verifyNote: Written from standard UK posterior eye practice (College of Optometrists, NICE NG81). Always check against Dr Aujla's slides and the current NICE guideline — referral thresholds and local pathways change.

topics.title: Direct ophthalmoscopy technique
topics.summary: From the week 3 PEG and week 5 AaM/PEG lectures: the direct ophthalmoscope gives a highly magnified (about 15x for an emmetrope), erect view of a small field. College guidance makes it the minimum internal examination on an undilated eye, so you need a fluent routine from the external eye to the macula and a descriptive way of recording it.
keyPoints: College guidance: as a minimum, examine internally with direct ophthalmoscopy on the undilated eye (other methods are allowed); if you can't get an adequate view, dilate or refer. The Opticians Act requires external and internal examination.
Set-up: lights off, glasses off, raise the chair, give a spotlight to fixate. Your right hand and right eye for their right eye; left for left. Explain that the light is bright and you'll come close.

Start with about +10 D (eye in focus at 10 cm, about 2.5x): red reflex, iris, pupil, cornea, lids and lashes (eyes closed), then the conjunctiva in each direction of gaze, reducing plus as you move through the media.

Posterior eye: find the disc (about 0 D if you're both emmetropic), check the posterior pole, then the periphery in 8 gaze directions (hold the upper lid in downgaze), and the macula last with the macular stop.
Magnification M = (K′ ÷ 4) × 1 ÷ (1 − wK): about 15x for an emmetrope, more for myopes, less for hyperopes.
Useful field of view j = g(K − W) ÷ K′: it shrinks with longer working distance, smaller pupils and myopia, and grows with hyperopia.
Apertures include wide, intermediate, macular stop, red-free, slit, fixation cross and cobalt blue.
Record descriptively for each structure (e.g. lids 'clean, full', cornea 'clear', iris 'brown, even colour'); avoid 'NAD', 'WNL' and 'normal'.
Direct ophthalmoscopy's advantages over indirect: an erect image, portability, and it suits every patient. Its limits: small field, no stereo, and it only reaches about the equator.
examTraps: Thinking field of view shrinks with hyperopia: it grows; it shrinks with myopia.
Saying a high myope must wear their glasses for the anterior eye: the patient's Rx doesn't matter there (it does help for the fundus).
Starting with the macula: the light constricts the pupil and makes the rest harder.
Reacting with surprise or alarm during the examination.

diagram.description: Top view of examiner and patient. Examiner's right eye is close to the patient's right eye, approaching from about 15° temporally. A dashed line shows the patient's line of sight to a distant target past the examiner's shoulder.

goDeeper.heading: Tips for hard cases
goDeeper.body: Small pupils: get as close as you can, turn the brightness down to reduce reflections, give clear fixation instructions, remind them it's fine to blink, and consider dilating. High myopes: let them wear their correction; everything looks big and the field is small, so it's easy to miss things, and they're at higher risk of detachment, so consider dilating or an indirect method.

goDeeper.heading: Monocular indirect ophthalmoscopes
goDeeper.body: The Welch Allyn PanOptic gives about 5x the field of a direct ophthalmoscope and the Keeler wide-angle about 10x. PanOptic routine: maximum aperture, centre the red dot on the filter dial, focus with the thumb lever and approach along the red reflex.

goDeeper.heading: Worked SAQ: field of view
goDeeper.body: +10.00 D eye, 4 mm pupil, 2.5 cm working distance: j = 0.004 × (10 − (−40)) ÷ 60 = 0.0033 m, about 3.3 mm.

topics.title: Slit lamp indirect ophthalmoscopy with condensing lenses
topics.summary: From the week 3 PEG lecture: slit lamp biomicroscopy with a high-plus condensing lens gives a stereoscopic, wide, variable-magnification view of the fundus. The image is real, aerial, inverted and laterally reversed. Know the indications, the lens powers, and the set-up.
keyPoints: Indications: symptomatic patients, a new patient, reduced VA (often unexplained), known retinal pathology, systemic disease with retinal effects, cataract and high myopia.
Binocular and stereoscopic, with a variable (potentially large) field, variable magnification and a longer working distance.

Lens table at a 16x slit lamp: SuperField and +90 D give 0.76x image magnification (about 12x) with a wide field; +78 D gives 0.93x (about 14x) with a narrower field; +60 D about 18x; +20 D gives 3x (used with headset BIO).
Lower-power lenses magnify more and have a narrower field.

Set-up: illumination in line with the microscope, moderate parallelepiped, low (10x) magnification, focus on the cornea, lens 5–11 mm from the eye (further for lower powers) with the 'V' pointing to the eye.
Pull the slit lamp back: the lens surface focuses first, then a blurred red reflex, then the fundus. Use all 8 positions of gaze for the periphery.
The −55 D Hruby lens gives a virtual, erect image but a field of only 5–8° (about a disc diameter) and is hard to keep in focus.
Advantages of binocular indirect over direct: stereo, larger field, beyond the equator, works through cataract and high ametropia, longer working distance.
examTraps: Forgetting the image is inverted and reversed when recording where a lesion is.
Holding the lens the wrong way round: the 'V' on a Volk lens points towards the eye.
Thinking higher-power lenses magnify more: they give a wider field and less magnification.

diagram.description: Side view: slit lamp beam passing through a handheld condensing lens into the eye; rays from the fundus emerge and form a real, inverted aerial image between the lens and the slit lamp, where the microscope focuses.

goDeeper.body: As magnification increases, field decreases. As Volk lens power decreases, magnification increases. For a first-time 21-year-old with no history, the lecture's answer is slit lamp biomicroscopy with a high-plus lens, because 'new patient' is an indication.

goDeeper.body: Dilating (e.g. tropicamide) gives a much better view, especially of the periphery; check the angle and IOP first, as in the week 5 and 9 lectures.

topics.title: Optic disc assessment
topics.summary: From the week 3 and week 5 PEG lectures: assess the disc for cup depth, rim colour, CD ratio, the ISNT rule, margins and any crescent or parapapillary atrophy, judging the cup by its contour and remembering that bigger discs have bigger cups.
keyPoints: What to record: CD ratio (vertical), cup depth (deep, medium, shallow), rim colour (pink/orange), margins (distinct or not), ISNT, and any crescent or parapapillary atrophy.
ISNT rule: the neuroretinal rim is usually thickest inferiorly, then superiorly, nasally and temporally. A disc that breaks it raises suspicion, especially with a large CD ratio.
Judge the cup by its contour (where the vessels bend), which can be larger than the colour cup (the pale area).
CD ratio rises with disc size (Blue Mountains Eye Study: average disc 1.5 mm), so a large cup in a large disc may be normal, and a CD of 0.6 may be non-pathological.
No cupping doesn't mean pathology: small discs often have little or no cup.
Glaucoma changes (week 11): progressive deepening and vertical enlargement of the cup, rim loss, and nasal displacement of the vessels.
Normal variations include myopic and choroidal crescents and a visible lamina cribrosa.
examTraps: Judging the cup by colour instead of contour.
Ignoring disc size when deciding if a CD ratio is abnormal.
Calling a disc with no cup abnormal.

diagram.description: Front view of an optic disc: outer disc margin, inner cup, neuroretinal rim between them labelled I, S, N, T with the rim thickest inferiorly and thinnest temporally. Vessels emerge from the cup and bend over the rim. A second smaller drawing shows an inferior notch with a flame haemorrhage at the margin.

goDeeper.heading: Worked SAQ: the ISNT rule
goDeeper.body: It describes the expected relative rim thickness: inferior thickest, then superior, nasal and temporal. It helps decide whether a disc with a large CD ratio is likely to be healthy.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: other glaucoma disc signs
goDeeper.body: Rim notching, disc haemorrhages (Drance), beta-zone parapapillary atrophy, baring of circumlinear vessels and bayoneting. A CD asymmetry over about 0.2 between similar-sized discs is suspicious. A pale rim (rather than cup) suggests a non-glaucomatous optic neuropathy, and swollen discs need urgent assessment.

Repeat IOP with Goldmann-type tonometry, do visual fields and OCT if available, and refer for suspected optic nerve damage (COAG/suspect) according to NICE NG81 and local pathways. cases.question: Explain the ISNT rule and why it may help in assessing optic nerve head health. [3]

It helps decide whether a disc with a large CD ratio is likely to be normal: a rim that breaks the pattern raises suspicion [1].

topics.title: Macula and retinal vessels: what normal looks like
topics.summary: From the week 5 AaM/PEG lecture: know what the normal macula and vessels look like, record them descriptively, and recognise common normal variations so you don't over-refer.
keyPoints: Macula: even colour, may look darker than the surrounding retina; foveal reflex present (often absent with age-related changes or drusen). The foveal reflex lies temporal to the disc.
A:V ratio describes relative vessel width, not number: arterioles are narrower, so 2:3 or 1:2 is normal (3:2 is not).
Look for nipping at crossings, tortuosity and narrowing: signs of systemic disease such as hypertension.
Normal variations: tigroid (tessellated) fundus, most often in myopes with thinner retinas; visible choroidal vessels; crescents.
Record the fundus and macula descriptively, e.g. 'even colour', 'foveal reflex present', 'A:V 2:3, even calibre, no nipping'.
examTraps: Saying a normal A:V ratio is 3:2.
Calling a tessellated myopic fundus abnormal.
Skipping the macula because the light is uncomfortable: switch to the macular stop and do it last.

diagram.description: Right fundus: optic disc on the right of the image (nasal), macula about two disc diameters to the left with a foveal pit at the centre. Four vascular arcades: superotemporal, inferotemporal, superonasal, inferonasal. Arteries drawn thinner and lighter, veins wider and darker.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: more on normal vessels
goDeeper.body: Arteries are lighter red with a brighter central light reflex; veins are wider and darker. At normal crossings the vein isn't narrowed or deflected. Spontaneous venous pulsation at the disc is seen in many normal eyes, but its absence alone isn't diagnostic.

topics.title: Tonometry: Goldmann applanation and non-contact
topics.summary: Goldmann applanation tonometry (GAT) is the reference standard for IOP. It flattens a 3.06 mm diameter area of cornea and uses the Imbert–Fick principle. Non-contact tonometry (NCT) is quicker and needs no anaesthetic, so it's widely used for screening.
keyPoints: Imbert–Fick principle: pressure = force ÷ area (W = P × A) for a thin, flat, dry membrane.
GAT flattens a 3.06 mm diameter area, where corneal rigidity and tear film surface tension roughly cancel out.
GAT needs topical anaesthetic and fluorescein; view with cobalt blue light.
End point: inner edges of the two green semicircles (mires) just touch; dial reading × 10 = mmHg.
Thick corneas over-read IOP; thin corneas under-read (CCT matters).
NCT: an air puff flattens the cornea; take several readings and average them.
Normal IOP is roughly 10–21 mmHg; it varies through the day (often highest in the morning).
examTraps: Mire rings too thick (too much fluorescein) → over-reading.
Pressing on the lids or the patient holding their breath, raising IOP.
Forgetting to disinfect the prism (or use a disposable tip).

diagram.description: Three views of the Goldmann mires through the slit lamp: (a) semicircles apart — IOP higher than the dial setting; (b) inner edges just touching — correct end point; (c) overlapping — dial set too high.
labels: Too low a setting: mires apart

goDeeper.heading: GAT step by step
goDeeper.body: Check for contraindications (e.g. corneal infection or abrasion, recent surgery), explain, instil anaesthetic and fluorescein, set the dial to about 10 mmHg, cobalt blue light with the beam fully open at about 60°, bring the prism gently to touch the central cornea, then adjust the dial until the inner edges of the mires meet. Read, multiply by 10, repeat, and record time and method.

goDeeper.heading: Corneal thickness and IOP
goDeeper.body: GAT assumes an average central corneal thickness (about 520–540 µm). Thick corneas resist flattening and give falsely high readings; thin corneas (including after refractive surgery) give falsely low readings. Thin CCT is also an independent risk factor for glaucoma. Don't use simple correction formulas as exact — consider CCT in your overall risk assessment.

goDeeper.heading: When NCT isn't enough
goDeeper.body: NCT can be affected by tear film, blinking and anxiety, and is less accurate at high pressures. Raised NCT readings should be repeated and confirmed with Goldmann-type (contact) tonometry before acting, in line with NICE NG81.

checklist.title: Goldmann applanation tonometry
steps: Check history: contraindications, allergies, CL wear (remove lenses).
Explain the procedure and get consent.
Disinfect the prism or fit a disposable tip; check calibration as per clinic protocol.
Instil topical anaesthetic and fluorescein.
Set cobalt blue light, wide beam, at about 60°; set the dial to about 10 mmHg.
Ask the patient to look straight ahead, eyes wide, breathe normally.
Bring the prism to the central cornea without touching lashes.
Adjust the dial until the inner edges of the mires touch.
Read (× 10 = mmHg), repeat, and do the other eye.
Record IOP, method and time; advise not to rub eyes while anaesthetised.

topics.title: Glaucoma: background and visual field analysis
topics.summary: From the week 11 visual fields lecture: glaucoma is an optic neuropathy with characteristic cupping and field loss, and IOP isn't part of the definition. Detect it with IOP, disc assessment and perimetry together from age 35, and read full-threshold fields systematically.
keyPoints: Classified by IOP: high-tension glaucoma, ocular hypertension, normal-tension and low-tension glaucoma. About 500,000 people in the UK have glaucoma.
Use the diagnostic triad (IOP, optic nerve head, perimetry) for everyone over 35, when risk becomes significant.

Mechanical theory: raised IOP compresses the lamina cribrosa and damages ganglion cell axons (doesn't explain normal-tension glaucoma). Vascular theory: reduced blood flow at the lamina causes ischaemia; low blood pressure adds risk.
Disc changes: deepening and vertical enlargement of the cup, rim loss, nasal vessel shift. Field defects: paracentral scotomas, enlarged blind spot, nasal step, arcuate scotoma.
Full-threshold perimetry is the standard for monitoring. Unreliable if fixation losses are over 20% or false negatives or positives over 33%.
MD reflects diffuse loss (e.g. cataract); PSD and CPSD reflect focal loss (e.g. glaucoma); beyond about ±2 dB is usually abnormal. The pattern deviation map reveals focal loss hidden under cataract.
Glaucoma hemifield test: compares mirror-image upper and lower sectors; outcomes are within normal limits, outside, borderline, general reduction or abnormally high sensitivity.

In England, first-degree relatives over 40 get free NHS sight tests. Risk factors include age, family history, Black African or Caribbean ethnicity, myopia and thin corneas.

topics.title: Fundus photography and OCT basics
topics.summary: Fundus photos document what you see and help spot change over time. OCT (optical coherence tomography) gives cross-sections of the retina and measures layer thickness — invaluable for the macula and for nerve fibre layer analysis in glaucoma, as long as you know its pitfalls.
keyPoints: Fundus cameras: typically 45° field; widefield systems image much more of the retina in one shot.
Red-free (green) photos improve contrast of vessels, haemorrhages and the nerve fibre layer.
OCT uses low-coherence interferometry with near-infrared light to make cross-sectional images (like ultrasound, but with light).
Retinal layers seen on OCT include RNFL, ganglion cell layer, photoreceptor layers (ellipsoid zone) and RPE.
Macular OCT shows fluid, drusen, epiretinal membranes, macular holes and thickness maps.
RNFL and ganglion cell analysis are compared with a normative database (green/amber/red).
Check scan quality, centration and segmentation before trusting the colours ('red disease' and 'green disease').
examTraps: Trusting the coloured normative map without checking scan quality.
Forgetting high myopes may fall outside the normative database.
Assuming a normal OCT rules out every disease.

diagram.description: Cross-sectional OCT of a normal macula: foveal pit in the centre, layers stacked from the vitreous side down: RNFL, ganglion cell layer, inner plexiform, inner nuclear, outer plexiform, outer nuclear, external limiting membrane, ellipsoid zone, RPE, choroid.

goDeeper.heading: Reading a macular OCT
goDeeper.body: Start with the foveal contour (is there a normal pit?). Then go layer by layer: anything above the retina (ERM, vitreomacular traction), within it (cysts, fluid), beneath it (subretinal fluid, drusen, PED). Compare the thickness map with the other eye and with previous scans.

goDeeper.heading: 'Red disease' and 'green disease'
goDeeper.body: Red disease: the scan flags thinning that isn't real (poor signal, segmentation errors, myopic eyes, floaters). Green disease: the scan looks normal but there's real pathology (early or focal loss, or a patient whose baseline was above average). Always combine OCT with the clinical picture, fields and photos.

topics.title: Peripheral fundus examination
topics.summary: Seeing the retinal periphery: head-mounted binocular indirect ophthalmoscopy, the slit-lamp contact fundus lens and scleral indentation, with their indications and set-up.
keyPoints: Head-mounted BIO with +20 D: stereoscopic, about 45° field, about 3x, real inverted and reversed image; can show the entire retina.
Contact fundus (mirror) lens: virtual, erect, reversed image with a limited field per mirror; needs topical anaesthetic and coupling fluid. Choose the mirror 180° from the area of interest.
Scleral indentation: patient supine, headset BIO and +20 D. The patient first looks away from the area, the indenter goes on the lid fold, then the patient looks towards it.
Indentation indications: far-peripheral lesions, symptoms, tobacco dust (Shafer's sign), vitreous haemorrhage, previous detachment, high myopia, or a periphery hard to see optically.
Landmarks: ora serrata about 7 mm behind the limbus; equator about 13–14 mm.
Light safety: keep the rheostat at half power and don't view one area for more than 40 seconds.
examTraps: Saying a contact fundus lens doesn't need anaesthetic because of the coupling gel. It does.
Having the patient look away from the indenter during indentation. They look towards it.
Doing scleral indentation upright, or saying it is only for active detachment.

goDeeper.body: Examples are oxybuprocaine 0.4%, tetracaine 0.5%, proxymetacaine 0.5% and lidocaine 4%. They are highly toxic so use them sparingly; proxymetacaine must be refrigerated. Record dose, batch number and expiry of any drug used.

topics.title: Pupils: testing and anomalies
topics.summary: A few quick tests (size in light and dark, direct and consensual responses, swinging flashlight, near response) sort pupil anomalies into afferent and efferent problems, and pick out the ones that need urgent referral.
keyPoints: Normal: equal, round, 2–4 mm in bright light and 4–8 mm in dim; smaller with age; not affected by sex, iris colour or refractive error.
Afferent defects (retina to pretectal area) cause an RAPD but not anisocoria. Efferent defects cause anisocoria but not an RAPD.
Swinging flashlight test: 2–3 seconds per eye, switching quickly; the eye with an RAPD dilates when lit. Cataract and refractive error never cause an RAPD.
No condition affects the near response while sparing the light response. Light-near dissociation: Adie's, Argyll Robertson, Parinaud's.
Anisocoria worse in bright light: parasympathetic (larger pupil abnormal, e.g. third nerve palsy, Adie's). Worse in the dark: sympathetic (smaller pupil abnormal, Horner's).
Physiological anisocoria (about 20% of people): usually under 1 mm, the same in light and dark, long-standing, normal reflexes.
Painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil: refer immediately (posterior communicating artery aneurysm). Acute change in pupil shape: refer immediately.
examTraps: Saying an RAPD comes with anisocoria. The consensual response keeps the pupils equal.
Calling Horner's a parasympathetic problem, or saying it is often bilateral.
Holding the light on each eye for less than 2–3 seconds during the swinging flashlight test, the commonest error.

goDeeper.heading: Drug tests
goDeeper.body: Pilocarpine 0.1% constricts an Adie's pupil (denervation supersensitivity) but not a pupil involved in third nerve palsy. Cocaine 4% blocks noradrenaline reuptake: it dilates a normal small pupil but has little effect on a Horner's pupil.

goDeeper.heading: Horner's syndrome
goDeeper.body: Mild ptosis (Müller's muscle), raised lower lid, miosis with dilation lag, normal light and near responses, reduced sweating on that side, and iris heterochromia if congenital. Causes include a Pancoast tumour, carotid aneurysm or dissection, and neck lesions. Refer to ophthalmology or neurology.

goDeeper.heading: Recording examples
goDeeper.body: Normal: PERRLA D+C, no RAPD, brisk, 4 mm R and L. Physiological anisocoria: round, reactive D+C and near, no RAPD, R 4 mm, L 3.5 mm. RAPD: RAPD +ve LE 0.4 log (quantified with ND filters).

flashcards.back: Pupils Equal, Round, Reactive to Light and Accommodation.

flashcards.front: Afferent versus efferent rule of thumb
flashcards.back: Afferent: RAPD, no anisocoria. Efferent: anisocoria, no RAPD.
Small, irregular, usually both eyes; light-near dissociation; neurosyphilis.
A blind eye: no direct response, and light in it gives no consensual response in the other eye. Light in the good eye constricts both.
Four neurons: retina to pretectal nucleus, to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, via III to the ciliary ganglion, then short ciliary nerves to the sphincter.

topics.title: Visual fields and where defects come from
topics.summary: The visual field maps onto the retina and visual pathway in an orderly way, so the shape of a defect and whether it matches between the eyes tells you roughly where the lesion is.
keyPoints: Normal monocular field: about 60° superior and nasal, 70° inferior, 100° temporal. Central field is 0–30°.
Physiological blind spot: 15° temporal to fixation, 1.5° below the horizontal, 5.5° wide and 7.5° high.
Scotoma: focal loss, relative or absolute. Diffuse loss is a general depression of the hill of vision.
Retinal nerve fibre lesions (e.g. glaucoma) give arcuate scotomas and nasal steps that respect the horizontal midline.

At the chiasm nasal fibres cross and temporal fibres don't. Pituitary adenoma, the commonest compressive lesion, gives bitemporal loss, often upper temporal first; a junctional scotoma comes from compression near Wilbrand's knee.
Lesions behind the chiasm give homonymous defects that respect the vertical midline and get more congruent the further back they are.
Stroke: a half to three-quarters of victims get field loss, most often homonymous hemianopia; any recovery is usually within a month.
Kinetic perimetry (moving target, about 4°/s) maps isopters; static perimetry (fixed positions, brightness varied) is more sensitive to shallow and small defects.
1 dB = 0.1 log unit; 0 dB is the brightest stimulus. Full threshold (4-2 dB staircase) quantifies; suprathreshold (about 5 dB above expected) screens but can miss shallow defects.
Grids: 24-2 or 30-2 (6° spacing) for glaucoma and neurology; 10-2 (2° spacing) for macular disease; Esterman for driving (UK: 120° horizontal).
SITA (Humphrey) uses Bayesian prediction: SITA Standard is as accurate as full threshold in about 7 minutes; SITA Fast matches FASTPAC in about 4. ZATA and GATE can start from previous results.
Reliability: fixation losses (blind spot checks or gaze tracking), false negatives (inflate loss) and false positives (hide loss).
Unreliable field: fixation losses over 20%, false negatives over 33% or false positives over 33%.
MD (mean deviation) reflects diffuse loss (e.g. cataract); PSD and CPSD reflect focal loss (e.g. glaucoma); beyond about ±2 dB is usually abnormal.
Total deviation shows all loss; pattern deviation removes general depression to show focal loss. The glaucoma hemifield test compares mirror-image upper and lower sectors.
examTraps: Forgetting the field is inverted and reversed on the retina: superior retinal damage gives an inferior field defect.
Expecting a homonymous defect from a lesion in front of the chiasm.
Relying on confrontation to rule out field loss: its sensitivity is only about 63%.
Comparing dB values between different perimeters: the scales aren't the same.

goDeeper.heading: Chiasmal tumours
goDeeper.body: Pituitary adenomas press from below: 6 mm of chiasmal elevation causes field defects in about half of cases and 11 mm in about 90%. Craniopharyngiomas, common in children, press from above and affect the superior nasal fibres first (inferior temporal field). Tuberculum sellae meningiomas mimic prefixed pituitary tumours.

goDeeper.heading: Macular sparing
goDeeper.body: About 80% of striate cortex represents the central 30°. Occipital lesions can spare the macula, which is hard to show with a 30-2 grid (6° spacing); use a 10-2 grid (2° spacing) or an Amsler chart.

flashcards.back: Homonymous: the same side of the field in both eyes (behind the chiasm). Heteronymous: opposite sides (e.g. bitemporal, at the chiasm).
Pituitary adenoma: bitemporal loss, reduced VA, disc pallor, colour defects.
How closely homonymous defects match between the eyes: more congruent the further back the lesion.

Full threshold: two crossings (4 then 2 dB), about 13 minutes an eye, more reproducible. Fast: one crossing (3 dB), about 8 minutes, more variable.
A fixed 10 dB stimulus not adjusted for eccentricity or age.
